subject: Science
title: The Cricket Match Clock: Understanding Speed and Time
hook: How fast is a ball traveling, and how do we measure motion?

image.alt: Motion and Time — Motion and Time

slides.title: The Fast Ball at the Match
slides.storyContext: During a village cricket match, a fast bowler releases the ball. It zooms past the batter in a blur. Coach Dev says: 'That's a 90 km/h ball.' Vikram asks: 'How do they know it's going 90 and not 80?' Sneha pulls out a notebook: 'It's about distance and time.'

image.alt: The Fast Ball at the Match — Motion and Time

slides.title: What Is Motion?

points.label: Definition
points.text: A change in position of an object relative to a reference point.

points.label: Reference point
points.text: An object or location we use to tell if something moved. A car moving at 60 km/h is fast relative to the ground but stationary relative to other cars on the highway.

points.label: Types
points.text: Uniform motion (same speed), non-uniform motion (changing speed).

slides.inSimpleWords: Motion is a change in where something is. Whether something moves depends on what you compare it to.

image.alt: What Is Motion? — Motion and Time

slides.title: Vikram Runs to the Store
slides.storyContext: Vikram decides to run to the store to buy supplies. He starts from home and runs 2 km toward the market. Then he realizes he forgot his wallet, so he runs 1 km back toward home. Finally, he gets the wallet and runs 2 km forward again to reach the market. Sneha watches and asks: 'How far did you actually travel, and how far are you from home?'

slides.title: Distance vs. Displacement

points.label: Distance
points.text: Total length of path traveled. Always positive. 'I walked 5 km around the village square.'

points.label: Displacement
points.text: Straight-line distance and direction from start to end. Can be zero if you return to start. 'I walked around the square and returned, displacement = 0 km.'

points.label: Example
points.text: Running 400 m on a circular track: distance = 400 m, displacement = 0 m.

example.problem: A delivery boy rides 3 km east to a house, then 4 km west back toward home. What is his distance and displacement?
example.solution: Distance = 3 + 4 = 7 km. Displacement = 3 − 4 = 1 km west.

slides.inSimpleWords: Distance is the full journey; displacement is the straight line from start to finish.

image.alt: Distance vs. Displacement — Motion and Time

slides.title: Vikram's Store Run Calculation
slides.storyContext: Let's calculate Vikram's actual journey.

example.problem: Vikram runs 2 km toward market, 1 km back home, then 2 km toward market again. What is total distance and final displacement?
example.solution: Distance = 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 km (add all segments). Displacement = 2 − 1 + 2 = 3 km from home toward market.

slides.title: Speed: How Fast Are You Going?

points.label: Definition
points.text: Speed = Total distance / Total time. Example: 100 km in 2 hours = 50 km/h.

points.label: Units
points.text: km/h (kilometers per hour), m/s (meters per second). To convert: 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h.

points.label: Average speed
points.text: Distance covered per unit time over a journey (may vary during journey).

points.label: Instantaneous speed
points.text: Speed at one exact moment (what a speedometer shows).

example.problem: A bus travels 240 km in 4 hours. What is its average speed?
example.solution: Speed = 240 km / 4 hours = 60 km/h.

slides.inSimpleWords: Speed tells you how much distance you cover per hour (or per second).

image.alt: Speed: How Fast Are You Going? — Motion and Time

slides.title: The Cricket Ball Speed Radar
slides.storyContext: At the cricket match, Coach Dev shows Vikram a radar gun. It measures how fast the ball travels. A ball bowled 22 meters (length of pitch) reaches the batter in 0.24 seconds. Coach Dev says: 'The faster the ball, the fewer seconds it takes. That's how we know speed.'

example.problem: A cricket ball travels 22 meters in 0.24 seconds. Convert to km/h.
example.solution: Speed = 22 m / 0.24 s = 91.67 m/s. Convert: 91.67 m/s × 3.6 = 330 km/h. (Note: this is unrealistic—actual bowling is ~30–35 m/s = 108–126 km/h, but math works the same way.)

slides.title: Velocity: Speed with Direction

points.label: Definition
points.text: Velocity = Displacement / Time, including direction. Example: '50 km/h north.'

points.label: Difference from speed
points.text: Speed is 'how fast'; velocity is 'how fast and which way.'

points.label: Example
points.text: Two cars: Car A: 60 km/h east. Car B: 60 km/h west. Same speed, opposite velocities.

slides.inSimpleWords: Velocity is speed plus direction. A GPS gives you velocity; a speedometer gives you speed.

image.alt: Velocity: Speed with Direction — Motion and Time

slides.title: The Direction Matters
slides.storyContext: Sneha explains to Vikram: 'Two runners on a circular track both run at 10 km/h, but one goes clockwise and one goes counterclockwise. Their speeds are the same, but their velocities are different—they're going in opposite directions.'

example.problem: Two cyclists ride on a straight road. Cyclist A travels 40 km north in 2 hours. Cyclist B travels 40 km south in 2 hours. Compare their speeds and velocities.
example.solution: Both have speed = 40 km / 2 hours = 20 km/h. But velocities: A = 20 km/h north, B = 20 km/h south. Same speed, opposite velocities.

slides.title: Acceleration: Speeding Up, Slowing Down, or Changing Direction

points.label: Definition
points.text: Change in velocity per unit time. Acceleration = (Final velocity − Initial velocity) / Time.

points.label: Types
points.text: Speeding up (positive), slowing down/deceleration (negative), changing direction (even at same speed).

points.label: Example
points.text: A car goes from 0 to 20 m/s in 5 seconds. Acceleration = 20 / 5 = 4 m/s².

example.problem: A cricket ball at rest is hit by a bat and reaches 30 m/s in 0.1 seconds. Find its acceleration.
example.solution: Acceleration = (30 m/s − 0 m/s) / 0.1 s = 300 m/s². (Very fast!)

slides.inSimpleWords: Acceleration is how quickly your speed or direction changes.

image.alt: Acceleration: Speeding Up, Slowing Down, or Changing Direction — Motion and Time

slides.title: Starting the Race
slides.storyContext: Vikram prepares for a 100-meter sprint. At the starting line, he accelerates from rest, reaching maximum speed midway through, then decelerates slightly at the end to avoid crashing into the finish line banner. Coach Dev watches with a stopwatch and notes how Vikram's speed changes throughout the race.

example.problem: Vikram runs a 100 m sprint. From 0–50 m, he accelerates from 0 to 10 m/s (50 m in 10 seconds). From 50–100 m, he maintains 10 m/s. What is his average acceleration in the first phase?
example.solution: Acceleration = (10 m/s − 0 m/s) / 10 s = 1 m/s². He speeds up at 1 meter per second every second.

slides.title: Understanding Non-Uniform Motion
slides.storyContext: Sneha explains: 'Not everything moves at the same speed. Vikram starts slow, speeds up, then tires out and slows down. That's non-uniform motion. The speedometer in a car changes constantly—that's why we have seatbelts for sudden acceleration and braking.'

slides.title: Uniform vs. Non-Uniform Motion

points.label: Uniform motion
points.text: Speed stays constant. A car on a highway at steady 60 km/h.

points.label: Non-uniform motion
points.text: Speed changes. A car accelerating, braking, or climbing a hill.

points.label: Real world
points.text: Most real motion is non-uniform. Uniform motion is rare and useful for calculations.

slides.inSimpleWords: Uniform = steady speed. Non-uniform = speed changing.

example.problem: A scooter travels 0–10 km at 20 km/h, then 10–30 km at 60 km/h. What is the average speed?
example.solution: First segment: 10 km at 20 km/h = 0.5 hours. Second segment: 20 km at 60 km/h = 0.33 hours. Total: 30 km in 0.83 hours = 36 km/h average.

slides.title: The Bus Journey
slides.storyContext: A local bus leaves at 8 AM to travel 60 km. It accelerates smoothly to 60 km/h in the first 10 minutes, maintains speed for 45 minutes, then brakes to a stop over 5 minutes. Sneha calculates whether this journey takes 1 hour.

points.label: Acceleration phase
points.text: 10 minutes at increasing speed averages ~30 km/h = 5 km.

points.label: Constant speed phase
points.text: 45 minutes at 60 km/h = 45 km.

points.label: Braking phase
points.text: 5 minutes from 60 km/h to 0 averages ~30 km/h = 2.5 km.

example.problem: Total distance = 5 + 45 + 2.5 = 52.5 km. With wait times at stops, does the journey take 1 hour?
example.solution: No. Just the motion takes ~1 hour. Add stops and it could be 1.5+ hours.

slides.title: Measuring Motion with Graphs
slides.storyContext: Coach Dev brings a distance-time graph to the next practice. He shows Vikram how a straight line means constant speed, while curves show acceleration or deceleration. 'The steeper the line, the faster you're going,' Coach says. Vikram realizes: 'So a flat line means I'm stopped!'

slides.title: Distance-Time Graphs

points.label: Horizontal line
points.text: Object is stationary (not moving).

points.label: Straight diagonal line
points.text: Constant speed. Steeper = faster.

points.label: Curve
points.text: Acceleration (speeding up or slowing down). Curves show non-uniform motion.

slides.inSimpleWords: On a distance-time graph, a steeper line means faster motion.

example.problem: A graph shows a straight line from (0, 0) to (2 hours, 100 km). What is the speed?
example.solution: Speed = 100 km / 2 hours = 50 km/h. The straight line indicates uniform motion.

slides.title: Motion Around Us
slides.storyContext: Sneha points out to Vikram: 'Look around. The wind is moving the leaves. Birds fly in curves—that's acceleration. The clouds drift slowly. The Sun moves across the sky. Even when you sleep, you're moving—Earth rotates!' Vikram laughs: 'Motion is everywhere!'

slides.title: Motion is Relative

points.label: Same object, different observers
points.text: A person sitting in a moving bus is at rest relative to the bus but moving relative to the ground.

points.label: Changing reference frame
points.text: Motion looks different from different viewpoints.

points.label: Why it matters
points.text: When we measure speed, we must always specify the reference (speed relative to what?).

slides.inSimpleWords: Motion is relative. Something can be still in one frame and moving in another.

example.problem: A person walks at 2 m/s inside a bus moving 20 m/s. What is their speed relative to the ground?
example.solution: If walking forward: 2 + 20 = 22 m/s. If walking backward: 20 − 2 = 18 m/s. Relative to the bus: 2 m/s always.

slides.title: The 400 m Race Analysis
slides.storyContext: Vikram runs a 400 m race on the school track in 1 minute (60 seconds). Sneha asks: 'What's your speed? Were you going the same speed the whole time?'

points.label: Average speed
points.text: 400 m / 60 s = 6.67 m/s or about 24 km/h.

points.label: Non-uniform motion
points.text: Vikram probably sprinted hard at the start, slowed midway, then pushed hard at the end.

example.problem: If Vikram ran the first 100 m in 12 seconds and the last 100 m in 16 seconds, did he accelerate or decelerate in the race?
example.solution: First 100 m speed = 100/12 = 8.33 m/s. Last 100 m = 100/16 = 6.25 m/s. He decelerated (slowed down) overall.

image.alt: The 400 m Race Analysis — Motion and Time

slides.title: Motion and Time Summary

points.text: Motion is change in position relative to a reference point.
Distance is total path; displacement is straight-line from start to end.
Speed = distance / time (scalar, no direction).
Velocity = displacement / time (vector, includes direction).
Acceleration is change in velocity over time (speeding, slowing, or direction change).
Uniform motion has constant speed; non-uniform motion has changing speed.

slides.inSimpleWords: Motion is measured by distance, speed, and time. Direction makes it velocity. Change means acceleration.

image.alt: Motion and Time Summary — Motion and Time

subject: Science
title: The Lightbulb Mystery: Current, Heat, and Magnets
hook: Why does a lightbulb get hot, and how does electricity make magnets?

image.alt: Electric Current and its Effects — Electric Current and its Effects

slides.title: Why Does the Bulb Glow?
slides.storyContext: During a power cut, Ravi uses a battery and flashlight. He wonders: 'Why does the filament glow when I switch it on? And why do nails stick to an electromagnet even when it's not a permanent magnet?' Divya invites him to her science club to find out.

slides.title: What Is Electric Current?

points.label: Definition
points.text: Flow of electric charge (usually electrons) through a conductor. Measured in amperes (A).

points.label: Conductor vs. insulator
points.text: Conductor: allows current to flow easily (copper, aluminum, water). Insulator: blocks current (rubber, plastic, glass).

points.label: Circuit needed
points.text: Current flows in a closed loop (circuit) from positive terminal of battery, through devices, back to negative terminal.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electric current is like water flowing through pipes—it needs a closed path to move.

image.alt: What Is Electric Current? — Electric Current and its Effects

slides.title: Ravi's First Experiment
slides.storyContext: Ravi connects a battery, wire, and bulb. Light! Then he tries breaking the wire—light goes out. He reconnects it—light returns. 'It's like a closed door—current can't get through if the door is open,' Mr. Kapoor explains. Ravi asks: 'What if I use two bulbs? Do they both light up equally?'

slides.title: Series vs. Parallel Circuits

points.label: Series
points.text: Bulbs/devices connected one after another in a single loop. If one bulb breaks, current stops and all go dark.

points.label: Parallel
points.text: Bulbs/devices connected on separate branches. Each gets full voltage. If one bulb breaks, others stay lit.

points.label: Home example
points.text: House lights are in parallel (each can switch on/off independently). Car lights were once series; now mostly parallel.

example.problem: Two bulbs in series powered by one battery. Brightness compared to one bulb alone?
example.solution: Each bulb gets half the voltage, so each is dimmer. Parallel: each bulb gets full voltage, so same brightness as one bulb alone.

slides.inSimpleWords: Series = one path (if one breaks, all stop). Parallel = many paths (one can break, others work).

example.problem: Three identical bulbs (each 3 V, 1 A) are connected to a 3 V battery. Compare brightness: (a) all series, (b) all parallel.
example.solution: (a) Series: each gets 1 V, dim. (b) Parallel: each gets 3 V, bright. Series bulbs are dim; parallel bulbs are bright.

slides.title: Design a Circuit for a Classroom
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor asks: 'How would you wire 10 lights in a classroom so each can switch on/off independently, and a burned-out bulb doesn't darken the whole room?' Ravi immediately knows: 'Parallel!'

slides.title: Thermal Effect of Current: Heat and Light

points.label: Joule heating
points.text: When current flows through a resistor, friction between moving electrons and atoms generates heat. Heat = I²Rt (Joule's law).

points.label: Incandescent bulb
points.text: Tungsten filament resists current heavily, gets red-hot (~2700 K), glows white. 95% energy wasted as heat.

points.label: Fuses and circuit breakers
points.text: Melt or trip when excessive current (short circuit) threatens to overheat wires and start fires.

slides.inSimpleWords: Current pushing through resistance creates heat and light. A thinner wire or tighter coil gets hotter faster.

image.alt: Thermal Effect of Current: Heat and Light — Electric Current and its Effects

slides.title: Why Does the Bulb Get Hot?
slides.storyContext: Divya holds a bulb (turned on) and pulls her hand back. 'Hot!' she says. Mr. Kapoor explains: 'The filament has high resistance. Current fighting through it heats it to ~2700 Kelvin. At that temperature, it glows white, and you feel the heat radiating.' Ravi asks: 'Why don't the wires connecting the battery get as hot?' 'Because they have low resistance,' Mr. Kapoor says. 'Most heat is generated where resistance is highest.'

example.problem: A bulb filament with resistance 100 Ω carries 0.5 A for 10 seconds. How much heat is generated? (Heat = I²Rt)

slides.title: Magnetic Effect of Current: Electromagnets

points.label: Magnetic field
points.text: Electric current flowing through a wire creates a magnetic field around it. Coil the wire and field strengthens.

points.label: Electromagnet
points.text: Wire coil around iron core + current = temporary magnet. Turn off current, magnetism stops.

points.label: Strength depends on
points.text: Current strength, number of coil turns, iron core presence.

example.problem: Why does wrapping wire around a nail multiple times make a stronger electromagnet than a single loop?
example.solution: More loops = magnetic field from each loop adds together. Iron core amplifies the combined field. Nail becomes temporary magnet.

slides.inSimpleWords: Coil a wire around a nail and run current through—the nail becomes a magnet as long as current flows.

slides.title: Ravi's Electromagnet
slides.storyContext: In the science club, Ravi wraps copper wire around a nail 20 times and connects it to a battery. 'Now touch it to paper clips,' Divya instructs. Ravi holds the electromagnet over paper clips and they jump up! He switches off the battery—the clips fall. 'It's magnetic, but only when current flows!' Ravi marvels. Mr. Kapoor nods: 'That's the difference from a permanent magnet. An electromagnet can be turned on and off.'

example.problem: An electromagnet with 50 coil turns around an iron nail picks up 30 paper clips. If you add another 50 turns (100 total), how many clips could it pick up (assuming current stays same)?
example.solution: Roughly double (to ~60 clips), because twice as many loops mean stronger combined field. Actual number depends on current and iron core saturation.

slides.title: Applications of Electromagnets

points.label: Electric bell
points.text: Electromagnet attracts a hammer, hammer strikes a bell, circuit breaks, electromagnet releases, spring returns hammer.

points.label: Relay
points.text: Small electromagnet controlled by switch opens/closes a separate high-power circuit.

points.label: Electric motor
points.text: Electromagnet in a magnetic field rotates, spinning an axle. Powers fans, drills, pumps.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electromagnets lift, ring, switch, and spin. No permanent magnet needed—just current.

image.alt: Applications of Electromagnets — Electric Current and its Effects

slides.title: The Electric Bell
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor shows a doorbell to the class. 'Press the button,' he says. When Ravi presses it, a hammer hits the bell—ding! 'That electromagnet pulls the hammer forward. But when it does, the circuit breaks, electromagnet releases, spring pushes hammer back, circuit reconnects, and the cycle repeats—ding, ding, ding!' Divya asks: 'So it rings continuously as long as I hold the button?' 'Exactly.'

slides.title: Real-World Electromagnets
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor takes students through the school. 'See the electric motor in the fan? Electromagnet. The relay in the circuit breaker? Electromagnet. The junkyard crane lifting scrap metal? Huge electromagnet.' Ravi realizes: 'Electromagnets are everywhere!'

slides.title: How an Electric Motor Works

points.label: Rotating coil
points.text: Electromagnet coil in a permanent magnetic field experiences forces that make it spin.

points.label: Commutator
points.text: Split ring that reverses current direction every half-rotation to keep coil spinning.

points.label: Speed control
points.text: More current = stronger rotation. More voltage = faster spin.

slides.inSimpleWords: A motor is an electromagnet spinning inside a permanent magnet's field.

slides.title: Design Your Own Electromagnet
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor challenges Ravi and Divya: 'Build an electromagnet that can lift 10 paper clips from a desk. You have copper wire, a nail, and a 1.5 V battery. What changes will make it stronger?'

points.label: Variables
points.text: Wire coil tightness, number of loops, battery voltage (use 2 batteries in series for 3 V), wire gauge (thickness).

points.label: Test method
points.text: Count paper clips lifted. More is better.

example.problem: Why does using 2 batteries (3 V) instead of 1 (1.5 V) make the electromagnet stronger?
example.solution: Higher voltage = more current through the coil = stronger magnetic field. The coil experiences more force.

slides.title: Resistance and Heating
slides.storyContext: Divya holds thick copper wire and thin nichrome wire, both connected to a battery. The thick wire stays cool; the thin wire glows red-hot. 'Thinner wire = higher resistance = more heat!' Mr. Kapoor explains. This is why toasters and heaters use thin wire.

slides.title: Resistance and Heat Generation

points.label: Resistance
points.text: Opposition to current flow. Thick wires: low resistance, cool. Thin wires: high resistance, hot.

points.label: Joule's law
points.text: Heat = I²Rt. More current, higher resistance, or longer time = more heat.

points.label: Practical uses
points.text: Toasters, heaters, electric ovens all use high-resistance wire to generate heat.

slides.inSimpleWords: Thin, high-resistance wire gets hotter than thick, low-resistance wire when the same current passes through.

slides.title: Current Matters in Electromagnets
slides.storyContext: Ravi builds two identical electromagnets but connects one to a fresh 1.5 V battery and another to an old, weak battery. The fresh battery electromagnet lifts 20 paper clips; the weak one lifts only 3. 'It's all about current!' Mr. Kapoor says. 'More current = stronger field.'

example.problem: Two electromagnets with 100 coil turns each: one with 0.5 A current, one with 1 A. How many times stronger is the second?
example.solution: Magnetic field strength is proportional to current. 1 A vs. 0.5 A = 2 times stronger. The second electromagnet can lift twice as many paper clips.

slides.title: Uses of Electromagnets in Daily Life

points.label: Doorbells and buzzers
points.text: Ring or buzz repeatedly when button held.

points.label: Microphones and speakers
points.text: Convert sound to current and back using electromagnets.

points.label: Magnetic locks
points.text: Hold doors shut with electromagnet; release when current cuts.

points.label: MRI machines
points.text: Powerful electromagnets create fields to image the human body.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electromagnets are used in almost every electrical device you touch.

slides.title: Safety with Electricity
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor shows the class a burned-out fuse. 'This saved a house from fire. When too much current flows (short circuit), the fuse melts and breaks the circuit before wires overheat and catch fire.' Ravi asks: 'How does the fuse know when there's too much current?' 'It melts when heat reaches a certain temperature,' Mr. Kapoor explains.

slides.title: Circuit Breakers and Safety

points.label: Fuse
points.text: Metal alloy that melts at high temperature, breaking circuit if current exceeds safe limit.

points.label: Circuit breaker
points.text: Automatic switch that trips (opens) when current exceeds safe level, preventing fire.

points.label: Earth/ground wire
points.text: Safety wire that carries excess current harmlessly into the ground if insulation fails.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fuses and circuit breakers protect you and your home from electrical fires.

slides.title: Electric Current and Its Effects

points.text: Electric current is flow of electrons through a closed circuit.
Series circuits share current (dim bulbs); parallel circuits share voltage (bright bulbs).
Current through resistance generates heat (Joule heating) and light (incandescent bulbs).
Current through a coil creates a magnetic field; coiled current is an electromagnet.
Electromagnets power bells, motors, relays, and many household devices.
Electromagnets turn on/off with current; permanent magnets cannot.

slides.inSimpleWords: Current heats and lights; coiled current creates magnets. No moving parts, just flowing electrons.

subject: Science
title: Aisha's Mirror Mystery: How Light Travels and Bounces
hook: Why do mirrors flip images, and why does a straw look bent in water?

image.alt: Light — Light

slides.title: The Straight Shadow
slides.storyContext: During an afternoon study session, Aisha holds a pencil in front of a lamp. The shadow on the wall is sharp and straight. She tilts the pencil—the shadow changes shape. Karan jokes: 'Light always travels in straight lines.' Aisha then puts a glass of water on the lamp and sees a straw inside look bent. 'That breaks your rule!' she says with a smile.

image.alt: The Straight Shadow — Light

slides.title: Light: What Is It?

points.label: Definition
points.text: Electromagnetic radiation that human eyes can see (wavelength 400–700 nanometers).

points.label: Source
points.text: Anything hot (Sun, flame, bulb filament) or fluorescent (glow stick, firefly).

points.label: Speed
points.text: Light travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s (300,000 km/s) in vacuum. Fastest thing known.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light is a wave of energy that travels in straight lines until it hits something.

image.alt: Light: What Is It? — Light

slides.title: The Speed of Light
slides.storyContext: Karan tells Aisha: 'Light travels so fast—300,000 km every single second. The light from the Sun takes 8 minutes to reach us. Light from the farthest stars takes years.' Aisha gasps: 'So I'm seeing the Sun as it was 8 minutes ago?'

slides.title: Rectilinear Propagation: Light Travels Straight

points.label: Definition
points.text: Light travels in straight lines in a uniform medium (same density).

points.label: Proof
points.text: Shadows are sharp-edged (not fuzzy). Pinhole camera creates inverted image. Laser beams are straight.

points.label: Exception
points.text: Light bends when entering a different medium (water, glass) due to change in speed.

example.problem: Why is the shadow of a pencil sharp on a wall close by but blurry on a wall far away during sunset?
example.solution: The Sun is a large source. Close wall: shadow edge sharp (blockage region small). Far wall: penumbra (partial shadow) grows large, so edge appears blurry.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light goes straight unless something stops it or it enters a new medium.

image.alt: Rectilinear Propagation: Light Travels Straight — Light

example.problem: A pinhole camera has a hole 1 cm in diameter. An object is 50 cm from the hole. Why does the image on the screen (50 cm behind hole) appear inverted?
example.solution: Light rays travel straight. Rays from the top of the object pass through the hole and hit the lower part of the screen. Rays from the bottom hit the top. This crossing inverts the image.

slides.title: Reflection: Light Bounces Off Mirrors

points.label: Law of reflection
points.text: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection (measured from the normal, a line perpendicular to the surface).

points.label: Plane mirror
points.text: Flat mirror creates a virtual image same size as object, same distance behind mirror, laterally inverted.

points.label: Curved mirrors
points.text: Concave mirrors focus light (used in telescopes). Convex mirrors spread light (used in car side mirrors).

example.problem: A person standing 2 meters from a plane mirror sees their image. How far behind the mirror does the image appear?
example.solution: Virtual image appears 2 meters behind the mirror (same distance as object is in front).

slides.inSimpleWords: Mirrors bounce light at the same angle it arrives. Your mirror image is behind the mirror, same distance as you are in front.

image.alt: Reflection: Light Bounces Off Mirrors — Light

slides.title: The Mirror Trick
slides.storyContext: Aisha looks in a mirror and waves. Her reflection waves back, same timing. She holds up a book and the reflection holds up a reversed book. Teacher Neha explains: 'The mirror isn't reversing left-right. It's reversing front-back. Your right hand looks like the reflection's left because we're looking at the back of the reflection.'

example.problem: Aisha stands 1.5 meters in front of a plane mirror. She walks 0.5 meters closer. How far is she from her image now?
example.solution: New distance from mirror = 1.5 − 0.5 = 1 meter. Image is 1 meter behind mirror. Total distance from Aisha to image = 1 + 1 = 2 meters.

slides.title: Curved Mirrors: Concave and Convex

points.label: Concave mirror (curved inward)
points.text: Converges light to focal point. Magnifies close objects. Used in telescopes, makeup mirrors.

points.label: Convex mirror (curved outward)
points.text: Diverges light, spreads it apart. Shows wider field of view. Used as car side mirrors, security mirrors.

points.label: Focal point
points.text: Point where reflected light rays meet (concave) or appear to come from (convex).

slides.inSimpleWords: Concave mirrors converge light and magnify. Convex mirrors spread light and show more area.

slides.title: The Magnifying Mirror
slides.storyContext: Aisha finds a makeup mirror and discovers her face appears magnified—but only when she's close. When she moves far, the image inverts and shrinks. Teacher Neha explains: 'That's a concave mirror. Its focus point controls the image size and direction.'

slides.title: Refraction: Light Bends in Water

points.label: Definition
points.text: Light bends when passing from one medium to another due to change in speed.

points.label: Rule
points.text: Light slows in denser media (water, glass), causing bend toward the normal. Light speeds up leaving denser media, bend away from normal.

points.label: Real vs. apparent
points.text: Straw in water appears bent. Fish underwater appear shallower than they are. This is refraction.

example.problem: Why does a fish in water appear at a different depth than it really is?
example.solution: Light from the fish bends upward as it leaves water (less dense → more dense, it bends toward normal). Our eye traces the ray backwards, placing the fish higher than reality.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light bends when it enters water because it slows down. This makes things underwater look closer than they really are.

image.alt: Refraction: Light Bends in Water — Light

slides.title: The Bent Straw
slides.storyContext: Aisha fills a glass with water and puts a straw in it. Looking from the side, the straw looks bent at the water surface! Karan says: 'But the straw isn't really bent—the light is.' Aisha asks: 'Why?' Teacher Neha explains: 'Light travels slower in water than in air. When light bends from air to water, it changes direction. That makes the straw appear bent where air meets water.'

example.problem: Light from the straw's submerged part travels up through water to Aisha's eye. Does it bend away from or toward the normal (vertical line)?
example.solution: Light travels slower in water (denser), so it bends toward the normal as it enters water from air, and away from the normal as it exits. Since we see light exiting water, it bends away from normal, making the straw appear higher than it really is.

slides.title: Lenses: Curved Glass Focuses Light

points.label: Converging lens (convex)
points.text: Thicker in middle, thinner at edges. Bends light rays toward a focal point. Used in magnifying glasses, cameras, microscopes.

points.label: Diverging lens (concave)
points.text: Thinner in middle, thicker at edges. Spreads light rays outward. Used in peepholes, to correct near-sightedness.

points.label: Focal length
points.text: Distance from lens to focal point. Shorter focal length = stronger magnification.

slides.inSimpleWords: A convex lens brings light together (magnifies or focuses). A concave lens spreads light apart.

slides.title: The Magnifying Glass
slides.storyContext: Karan brings a magnifying glass to show Aisha how it magnifies small print. When she moves the glass closer to the paper, the text appears larger and sharper. When she moves too far away, the image disappears. 'There's a sweet spot,' Teacher Neha explains. 'That's the focal point of the lens.'

example.problem: A converging lens has focal length 5 cm. An object 10 cm from the lens creates an image. Is the image real or virtual, and how many times magnified?
example.solution: Object at 2× focal length creates a real, inverted image at 2× focal length on the other side. Magnification = 1× (same size). This is used in copy machines.

slides.title: The Candle and the Lens Experiment
slides.storyContext: Teacher Neha brings a convex lens and a candle. She places the lens between candle and wall, adjusts distance. A real, inverted image of the candle appears on the wall. Aisha asks: 'How is the image upside-down? And how is it bright without electricity?'

points.label: Real image
points.text: Light rays actually converge at a point on screen. Upside-down (inverted) because light rays cross at focal point.

points.label: Virtual image
points.text: Rays don't converge; eye traces rays backward (mirror, magnifying glass). Same way up as object.

example.problem: Using a convex lens, object at 2× focal length creates an image. Where and how large?
example.solution: Image appears at 2× focal length on opposite side, inverted, same size as object. Used in copy machines and projectors.

slides.title: Applications of Lenses
slides.storyContext: Karan shows Aisha his telescope and camera. 'Lenses in both,' he says. 'Telescope focuses distant starlight to my eye. Camera focuses sunlight onto film to capture images.' Teacher Neha adds: 'Glasses correct vision by using lenses to refocus light on your retina. Microscopes magnify tiny objects using multiple lenses together.'

slides.title: Real vs. Virtual Images

points.label: Real image
points.text: Light rays converge at actual point (screen can show it). Inverted. Example: projector, camera.

points.label: Virtual image
points.text: Light rays don't converge; eye traces them backward to a point. Upright. Example: mirror, magnifying glass.

points.label: When it matters
points.text: Real images can be displayed on screens. Virtual images can only be seen by looking through the lens.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real images appear on screens (inverted). Virtual images appear behind mirrors or in lenses (upright).

slides.title: Correcting Vision with Lenses
slides.storyContext: Aisha's friend wears glasses. Teacher Neha explains: 'If your eye naturally focuses light behind the retina (farsighted), a convex lens bends light inward. If light focuses in front of the retina (nearsighted), a concave lens spreads it. Glasses correct where light lands.'

example.problem: Aisha is nearsighted and cannot see far objects clearly. Light from a distant tree focuses in front of her retina. Which lens type corrects this?
example.solution: Concave lens. It diverges (spreads) incoming light so it focuses farther back, now on the retina where it should.

slides.title: Color and Light

points.label: Visible spectrum
points.text: Wavelengths 400–700 nm: red (700 nm), orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet (400 nm).

points.label: Primary colors of light
points.text: Red, green, blue (RGB). Mix to make any color. All together = white.

points.label: White light
points.text: Combination of all visible colors. Prism separates white into spectrum.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light has different colors depending on its wavelength. Mix them and you get new colors.

slides.title: The Rainbow Prism
slides.storyContext: Karan brings a prism. When white sunlight enters, it separates into a rainbow of colors on the wall. Aisha gasps: 'White light contains all colors!' Teacher Neha nods: 'Each color bends slightly differently in glass, so they separate.'

example.problem: White light enters a prism. Red light bends less, violet bends more. Why?
example.solution: Violet has shorter wavelength (higher frequency). Shorter-wavelength light bends more in glass. Red's longer wavelength bends less.

slides.title: Light and Optics Summary

points.text: Light travels in straight lines in uniform media (rectilinear propagation).
Reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection (mirrors).
Refraction: light bends when entering a new medium (water, glass).
Mirrors create virtual images (same way up). Lenses create real or virtual images.
Convex lenses converge light (magnify, focus). Concave lenses diverge light.
Curved mirrors and lenses focus or spread light depending on their shape.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light bounces off mirrors, bends in water, and focuses through lenses. Understanding these rules explains why the world looks the way it does.
